name: Aaron Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Aaron. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and this is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a maintenance electrician for Keystone, a facilities company, so I look after supermarkets, offices and a couple of gyms across the north side of the city. A normal day is a list of call-outs on my phone: a freezer circuit tripping at a supermarket, emergency lighting tests at an office block, a hand dryer that's set fire to itself. I like that every day's different and I'm not stuck on one building site. The worst bit is the night call-outs, two in the morning in a car park, because a fridge alarm went off.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Leila, who teaches at a primary school, and we rent a house. My brother and I own a small flat together that we rent out, and I've got about eight months of savings on top. I use ChatGPT now and then, mostly to look up odd fault codes on fridge controllers. I'm pretty middle of the road about most things, I just like to see something work before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool and not much more, which is what I've always thought. At work we'd joke that the fault-code lookup is the only useful thing it does. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, and a bit smug. My work is hands-on and spread across dozens of buildings, so it was never in danger. If nothing changes, I'm in a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Keystone and keep saving. I'd maybe do a course in building controls, the systems that run heating and lighting in big buildings, because they pay more. And we'd keep the rental flat ticking along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Keystone already use AI for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They use a system that sends jobs to our phones and picks who's closest. It's handy, though it sometimes sends me across the city for a five-minute job. If AI only improves that, great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else worrying you about the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rental flat, a bit, because the tenant's moving out and the boiler is on its last legs. And Leila's school might merge with another one. Neither's a disaster.

say: I'd say AI is a **handy tool** and not much more.
We'd joke that **fault-code lookup** is the only useful thing it does.
think: My work is **hands-on** across dozens of buildings, so it was never in danger.
If nothing changes, I'm in a **good spot**.
do: Carry on at **Keystone** and keep saving.
Maybe do a **building controls** course, since it pays more.
Keep the **rental flat** ticking along with my brother.
feel: **Calm**, because nothing here touches my work.
S0.quote: A hand dryer in an office toilet doesn't care how clever the computer is, it still needs someone with a screwdriver.
fieldNote: Aaron's job is **mobile maintenance** across many sites, with little thinking work.
His small worries are **landlord** ones: a tenant leaving and an old boiler.
He trusts things **once they work**, which shapes his calm here.

steps.text: Keep doing call-outs for Keystone across the north side
Look into a building controls course for better pay
Replace the old boiler in the rental flat before new tenants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change things for the office side, and we should get ahead of it. I'd say the trades will be fine but the jobs might change. I'd probably say it a bit more quietly than some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's a mixed bag. The planning and booking side at Keystone would be AI, so the job system gets smarter and maybe sends us out with fewer people. And if offices shrink, there are fewer offices for us to maintain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the building controls course this year, because the smart systems in buildings need someone who understands both the wiring and the software. I'd learn the new tools Keystone brings in once the other lads have tried them. I'd save a bit more, maybe stop eating out so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Keystone would feel this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The help desk, the planners and the estimators. And maybe some of us, if the system works out it needs eight sparks instead of ten. I'm middle of the team, so I wouldn't want to be one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the rental flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably fine, because people still need somewhere to live. Maybe the tenant would be someone who just lost an office job, which is a worry for rent. I'd keep a few months of the rent aside in case.

say: I'd say the **office side** will change, and we should get ahead of it.
I'd say the **trades** will be fine, but the jobs might change.
think: Keystone's **job system** gets smarter and might send out fewer electricians.
If offices shrink, there are **fewer offices** for us to maintain.
do: Do the **building controls** course this year.
Learn Keystone's **new tools** once the other lads have tried them.
Save a bit more and **eat out** less.
S1.quote: If the system works out Keystone needs eight sparks instead of ten, I'm middle of the team, so I wouldn't want to be one of the two.
fieldNote: Aaron sees the risk inside his firm: smarter **dispatch** may mean fewer electricians.
He reaches for **building controls**, a mix of wiring and software.
His landlord side adds a quiet worry about **tenants'** jobs.

steps.text: Sign up for a building controls course this year
Learn Keystone's new dispatch tools after colleagues try them
Set aside three months of rental income as a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to think about this calmly and not panic. I'd tell people with savings to hold on to them. I'd probably keep quiet online, because people get nasty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a lot. In 2028 the office tenants go, so offices empty and supermarkets cut staff, and then in 2031 robots arrive that could do half my call-outs. I'm thirty-one then, renting, with a teacher's wage and a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build savings up from eight months to twelve. I'd do the building controls course fast, because the systems will still need someone to fix them when they break. And I'd talk to my brother about whether to keep the flat or sell it while prices hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a cushion, but it's a short cushion for that kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my three years to get onto the right side. Thinking AI will run the dispatch and the planning, but the robots aren't there yet, so I still have work. I'd want to be the one who fixes the robots and the building systems by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If house prices looked like they'd drop, I'd rather sell while they're up and keep the cash. But my brother's more stubborn than me, so we'd argue about it for a month.

say: I'd tell people to think **calmly** and not panic.
I'd tell anyone with **savings** to hold on to them.
think: In 2028 offices **empty** and supermarkets cut staff, so call-outs drop.
In **2031** robots could do half my call-outs, when I'm thirty-one and renting.
do: Build savings from **eight to twelve** months.
Decide with my brother whether to **sell the flat** while prices hold.
feel: **Anxious**, because my cushion is **short** for this much change.
S2.quote: Thinking AI will run the dispatch and the planning, but the robots aren't there yet, so I still have work for three years.
fieldNote: Aaron sees a **three-year window** to move into fixing robots and building systems.
His **rental flat** becomes a sell-or-hold decision.
He'd keep a **calm public face** while privately anxious.

steps.text: Build savings from eight to twelve months of costs
Finish the building controls course within a year
Agree with his brother whether to sell the rental flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan if we start now. I'd say firms like Keystone should be training people up instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2034, so I'm thirty-four. That's a lot better. I'd have time to get qualified in building controls and maybe in robotics maintenance if that becomes a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the course, keep the flat, keep saving. I'd look at the AI tools more seriously in a couple of years, once they've settled. And Leila and I would probably still buy our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. More like a plan than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say teachers are safer than sparks, which might be true. She'd also say stop reading the news before bed. She keeps me level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I act in a hurry or properly. With five years, I'd watch what works, then commit. That's how I do most things.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan** if we start now.
Firms like Keystone should be **training people** instead of waiting.
think: Robots by **2034** is a lot better for me.
I'd have time for **building controls** and maybe **robot maintenance**.
do: Do the **controls course** and keep the flat and savings.
Take the **AI tools** seriously in a couple of years.
Still **buy our own place** with Leila.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more like a **plan** than a panic.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd watch what works, then commit. That's how I do most things.
fieldNote: Leila's **teaching job** feels like the safer anchor to him.
He'd still go ahead with **buying a home**.

steps.text: Finish the building controls course over two years
Buy a house with Leila on their two incomes
Start using AI fault-finding tools once they settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if people are sensible. I'd say the same to my mates, just don't leave it to the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2039, I'm thirty-nine. I'd have time to move into controls or robot maintenance comfortably. I think I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, but with a plan. Controls course in the next couple of years, buy a house, keep the rental flat. Maybe add a second rental flat if the money's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start now, with ten years ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The controls course, definitely. And I'd start putting a bit away every month into a pension, which I've been lazy about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Keystone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if a building controls firm offered more. I'm not loyal to a company, I'm loyal to a pay slip. But I'd only move once I'd seen the new job was solid.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** if people are sensible.
I'd tell mates not to **leave it** to the last minute.
think: Robots by **2039** gives me time to move into **controls** comfortably.
do: Do the **controls course** in the next couple of years.
**Buy a house** and keep the rental flat, maybe adding another.
Start paying into a **pension** every month.
S4.quote: I'm not loyal to a company, I'm loyal to a pay slip.
fieldNote: Aaron would use ten years to build **assets**: a home, rentals, a pension.
He's **pragmatic** about employers and would move for pay.
His mood here is **uneasy at the edges**, not anxious.

steps.text: Take the building controls course within two years
Buy a second rental flat with his brother if prices suit
Start monthly payments into a personal pension

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have time to get to the other side. What would help is firms like Keystone paying to retrain us on controls and robots, and clear warnings about which jobs are going so I can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to buildings. If offices empty, half my work goes even before a robot arrives. A hand dryer in an office toilet doesn't care how clever the computer is, it still needs someone with a screwdriver, but only if someone's still using that office.

headlineQuote: If offices empty, half my work goes even before a robot arrives.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** maintenance electrician at Keystone, covering supermarkets, offices and gyms.
He lives with **Leila**, a primary teacher, and co-owns a **rental flat** with his brother.
He's **steady**: he tries tools only once he sees them work.
He sees his risk in **emptying offices** and smarter dispatch before robots.
With more time he'd move into **building controls** and build up assets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he wouldn't have time to reach safer work.
whatWouldHelp: Employers paying to **retrain** electricians on controls and robots.
Clear **warnings** about which jobs are going.
